x.A: A NAT gateway in each AZ's public subnet, with a private route table per AZ that sends non-VPC traffic to the NAT gateway in the same AZ, gives private instances outbound internet access. It stays available if one AZ fails.
x.B: NAT instances need to be patched, sized, and failed over by hand, which is more operational work than managed NAT gateways. They also should be in public subnets, not private ones.
x.C: A VPC can have only one internet gateway, and an internet gateway attaches to the VPC, not a subnet. It also would not hide private instances.
x.D: An egress-only internet gateway works for IPv6 only. This VPC uses IPv4 CIDR blocks.

x.A: The EC2 instance's location relative to the EFS file system's AZ does not help to transfer or automate the data. EFS is Regional and mount targets exist in every AZ.
x.B: A DataSync agent installed on premises reads from the NFS-based source and sends data securely and automatically to AWS.
x.C: A secondary EBS volume is not needed because the data must be stored in EFS, not on the instance.
x.D: Manually copying with an OS command is not an automated approach.
x.E: DataSync needs a source location configuration for the on-premises server and a destination location for EFS. With the agent, the transfer can be scheduled and automated.

x.A: Job bookmarks let Glue remember which data it has already processed, so later runs process only new data.
x.B: Deleting the data after processing removes data the company may still need, and it is not the way to avoid reprocessing.
x.C: Setting NumberOfWorkers to 1 changes capacity and speed, not which data is processed.
x.D: FindMatches finds duplicate records within the data, and it doesn't track which files were already processed.

x.A: Shield Advanced protects against large-scale DDoS attacks on resources like CloudFront, ELB, and Elastic IPs, and gives access to the AWS DDoS response team.
x.B: GuardDuty detects threats and generates findings. It does not automatically block attackers.
x.C: CloudFront with static and dynamic content absorbs traffic at edge locations worldwide, so attack traffic is spread out before it reaches the web servers.
x.D: Network ACLs have a limited number of rules, so they cannot hold thousands of attacker IP addresses, and this approach reacts slowly.
x.E: Spot Instances can be reclaimed, so they are a poor choice when downtime is not acceptable, and scaling on CPU does not stop an attack.

x.A: An execution role is for what the function can do, not who can invoke it. Using * as principal is also not least privilege.
x.B: An execution role does not control who invokes the function, and lambda.amazonaws.com is not the service that invokes it from EventBridge.
x.C: A resource-based policy is correct, but allowing lambda:* grants far more actions than needed, so it breaks least privilege.
x.D: A resource-based policy on the function that allows only lambda:InvokeFunction for the events.amazonaws.com service principal gives EventBridge exactly the permission it needs.

x.A: SSE-C means the company supplies and manages its own keys, and there is no automatic key rotation or key usage log.
x.B: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3 and key usage is not logged to CloudTrail for the customer, and you cannot control rotation.
x.C: SSE-KMS logs key use to CloudTrail, but manual rotation adds operational work every year.
x.D: SSE-KMS encrypts the data at rest, key usage is logged in CloudTrail, and automatic rotation rotates the key every year with no manual work.

x.A: Athena queries data in S3 with SQL but does not offer a REST API for storing and retrieving location data.
x.B: API Gateway provides the REST API and Lambda stores and retrieves the location data, so the existing analytics platform can use it. It scales during peak hours.
x.C: QuickSight with Redshift is for analytics dashboards and is not a REST API for location data.
x.D: Kinesis Data Analytics processes streams with SQL or Flink and is not a store that can be retrieved through a REST API.

x.A: A Lambda function triggered by a database update is hard to do natively for RDS, and sending to a single SQS queue means the targets would compete for the same messages rather than each receive a copy.
x.B: A FIFO queue has the same problem, because each message is consumed by only one consumer, so multiple targets cannot all receive it.
x.C: This reverses the fan-out pattern. SQS does not fan out to SNS topics.
x.D: An RDS event notification published to an SNS topic fans out to multiple SQS queues, so each target system gets its own copy of the message, and Lambda functions update the targets.

x.A: A Glacier vault lock applies to Glacier vaults, not S3 buckets, and a WORM vault lock policy cannot be undone, and it also has a fixed retention.
x.B: Governance mode with a 100 year retention period is a fixed period, not an indefinite hold, and users with bypass permission can still delete.
x.C: CloudTrail only notifies after an object is modified. It does not prevent change.
x.D: Object Lock with versioning and a legal hold keeps objects unchangeable for an unspecified time until the hold is removed. Only users with the s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission can remove it.

x.A: Uploading to S3 Glacier does not make uploads faster and Glacier is an archive tier, so it doesn't help.
x.B: Having the web server upload originals to S3 still means the upload passes through the web servers, so the performance problem remains.
x.C: A presigned URL lets the browser upload straight to S3, which removes the load from the web servers and decouples the upload from the application.
x.D: An S3 event notification invokes Lambda to resize the image after it is uploaded. This decouples resizing from the upload and scales automatically.
x.E: A scheduled Lambda is not event-driven, so images wait until the next run, and it requires polling for new uploads.

x.A: A self-managed second ActiveMQ and a replicated MySQL on EC2 both require manual failover and management, which is not low operational complexity.
x.B: Amazon MQ is good, but replicating MySQL on EC2 is still manual and does not provide automatic failover.
x.C: Amazon MQ and RDS Multi-AZ are good, but a single extra consumer instance is manual and doesn't scale or replace failed instances automatically.
x.D: Amazon MQ with active/standby brokers across two AZs, an Auto Scaling group of consumers across two AZs, and RDS Multi-AZ make every tier highly available with automatic failover and replacement.

x.A: Fargate on ECS runs the existing containers with minimal changes, Service Auto Scaling handles growing requests, and an ALB distributes traffic. There are no servers to manage.
x.B: Two fixed EC2 instances would require managing hosts and would not scale with growing requests.
x.C: Lambda would require rewriting the application, which goes against minimum code changes.
x.D: An HPC cluster is meant for tightly coupled compute jobs and is a poor fit for a web application, and it is heavy to operate.

x.A: DataSync would send 50 TB over the network, but the data center has no available bandwidth.
x.B: A Snowcone holds only 8 TB or 14 TB, so it can't hold 50 TB, and it is not meant to run the full transformation application.
x.C: A Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device holds enough data and moves it offline without using network bandwidth. A Glue job in AWS can then run the weekly transformation with little operational work.
x.D: Running the application on the device's compute and then recreating it on EC2 adds unnecessary complexity and operational work.

x.A: DynamoDB has a small item size limit (400 KB), so it is not suitable for storing photos.
x.B: Firehose delivers streaming data and does not process photos or store them with metadata.
x.C: Lambda scales automatically to process photos, S3 stores the photos at any scale, and DynamoDB keeps the metadata. This scales with varying numbers of users.
x.D: Three EC2 instances with EBS volumes is a fixed capacity, so it does not scale to variable demand.

x.A: A NAT gateway sends traffic out through the internet gateway, so the traffic still goes over the internet.
x.B: A security group restricting outbound traffic limits where traffic can go, but does not change the path, so it still goes over the internet.
x.C: Moving the instances to private subnets and adding an S3 gateway VPC endpoint linked to the route table sends file transfers to S3 over the AWS private network.
x.D: Removing the internet gateway and adding Direct Connect is a heavy and costly change, and Direct Connect to a public service like S3 requires a public virtual interface.

x.A: CloudFront in front of the site provides HTTPS, global caching, scalability, and edge security with little work.
x.B: AWS WAF filters web requests, but it does not provide HTTPS functionality.
x.C: A Lambda function to serve the content would require building and maintaining code, and is not needed for a static website.
x.D: A static website that changes four times a year can be hosted on S3 with static website hosting, which is highly scalable and has no servers to patch.
x.E: EC2 with Auto Scaling and an ALB requires patching and maintenance, which is exactly the burden the company wants to remove.

x.A: A CloudWatch Logs subscription can stream log data to OpenSearch Service directly in near real time, with little configuration and no code.
x.B: A custom Lambda function means writing and maintaining the code to write logs to OpenSearch.
x.C: Firehose can deliver to OpenSearch, but a CloudWatch Logs log group cannot be configured directly as a Firehose source this way, and the extra service adds setup.
x.D: Installing the Kinesis Agent on every server is much more operational work, and it is not needed because the logs are already in CloudWatch Logs.

x.A: EBS volumes have size limits and attach to one instance in one AZ, so they cannot scale to 900 TB for multi-AZ web servers.
x.B: EFS can scale to this size and be shared by multiple AZs, but its storage cost is much higher than S3.
x.C: OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine, not cost-effective bulk storage for 900 TB of text documents.
x.D: S3 scales without limit, stores data across multiple AZs, and has the lowest cost per GB of these options for a large document repository.

x.A: AWS WAF in each Region protects against SQL injection and XSS, but you would configure it separately in every account and Region, which is more administrative effort.
x.B: Firewall Manager lets you centrally configure AWS WAF rules across accounts and Regions, so the same SQL injection and XSS protections apply with the least administrative effort.
x.C: Shield protects against DDoS attacks, not SQL injection or cross-site scripting.
x.D: Shield in one Region doesn't protect against SQL injection or XSS, and it leaves the other Region unprotected.

x.A: Geolocation routing with Route 53 and CloudFront does not work well for DNS traffic over UDP and TCP port 53, because CloudFront serves HTTP and HTTPS.
x.B: A standard accelerator in Global Accelerator has endpoint groups in us-west-2 and eu-west-1, with the NLBs as endpoints. It supports TCP and UDP traffic and routes users to the closest healthy endpoint.
x.C: Attaching Elastic IPs to six instances and using CloudFront cannot serve DNS traffic, and the setup is complicated and not highly available.
x.D: ALBs support only HTTP and HTTPS, so they cannot handle DNS traffic, and CloudFront does not support DNS.

x.A: You cannot encrypt an existing RDS instance in place, but you can copy the latest snapshot with encryption and restore it as a new, encrypted DB instance. Future snapshots from that instance are encrypted too.
x.B: RDS manages its own storage, so you can't create your own EBS volume and attach it. Encryption cannot be enabled on an existing DB instance.
x.C: A restore always creates a new DB instance. You cannot restore a snapshot onto an existing instance.
x.D: Copying snapshots to an S3 bucket doesn't make the database or future snapshots encrypted.

x.A: MFA protects sign-in and is not a key management infrastructure.
x.B: KMS is a managed service to create and control encryption keys that scales, integrates with AWS services, and logs usage, so it reduces the operational burden.
x.C: ACM manages TLS/SSL certificates, not encryption keys for application data.
x.D: An IAM policy limits who can use keys, but it does not create or manage them.

x.A: Installing a certificate from ACM on each instance still leaves SSL termination on the instances, and ACM certificates can't be exported for installation on EC2.
x.B: Certificates in S3 can't be used for SSL termination by EC2 instances.
x.C: A proxy server with the certificate would just move the load to another instance that you manage and must scale.
x.D: Importing the certificate into ACM and attaching it to an ALB HTTPS listener moves SSL termination to the load balancer, freeing up the web servers' CPU.

x.A: The job is stateless, interruptible, and runs for about an hour, so Spot Instances give the largest savings and scale easily.
x.B: Reserved Instances suit steady, long-running workloads. A dynamic batch job doesn't run constantly, so it would waste money.
x.C: On-Demand Instances work, but they cost more than Spot for an interruptible job.
x.D: Lambda has a 15 minute limit, so a 60 minute job can't run on it.

x.A: Instances in private subnets with Auto Scaling and a Multi-AZ RDS in private subnets keeps them off the public internet and highly available.
x.B: An Application Load Balancer that faces the internet must sit in public subnets, not private ones.
x.C: Instances in public subnets would be exposed to the internet, which the requirements don't allow.
x.D: Two public subnets with the ALB, two private subnets for the instances, and two NAT gateways in two AZs let the instances reach the payment service without being exposed, and the design stays highly available.
